Bones of the Vertebral Column the regional vertebra — and how shape dictates movement

Every lecture slide, shown in full and explained like a tutor would. The organising idea: once you know the typical vertebra (from L17), each region is just a set of modifications that trade mobility for load-bearing or for protecting what passes through — so read every feature as "what does this let the region do, and what passes here?"

§1Cervical region

Cervical vertebrae (C1–C7)

The most mobile region — and the one with its own artery tunnel.

Seven small vertebrae built for range of motion. The region's signature is the transverse foramen (unique to the cervical spine), and three of the seven are atypical — the atlas, the axis and the vertebra prominens. Learn the identifying features as a checklist.

Why · built for the widest range of movement

Cervical vertebrae are the smallest of the 24 movable vertebrae, and three design choices make the neck the most mobile region: relatively thick IV discs, near-horizontal articular facets (which permit gliding in many directions), and little surrounding body mass. The trade-off is stability — the same mobility is why the cervical spine is so vulnerable in whiplash and high-energy trauma.

Exam hook · the cervical identification checklist

Spot a cervical vertebra by: a small, wide body; a large triangular vertebral foramen (roomy because the cervical cord enlargement sits here); a transverse foramen in each transverse process (transmits the vertebral artery, C6→C1); anterior and posterior tubercles on the transverse process (the C6 anterior tubercle is the carotid tubercle, used to compress the carotid); a bifid spinous process (C2–C6); and uncinate processes (raised lateral lips of C3–C6) that form the uncovertebral joints.

Why · the top two are purpose-built for head motion

The atlas (C1) is a ring with no body and no spinous process — its lost body became the dens of C2. It cradles the skull on two large facets, giving the "yes" nod at the atlanto-occipital joint. The axis (C2) projects the dens (odontoid process) upward as a pivot, around which the atlas (and the skull) rotate for the "no" shake. These two joints are detailed in the L20 craniovertebral guide.

Clinical · C7, the landmark you can feel

C7 is the vertebra prominens — its long, non-bifid spinous process is the bony lump you feel at the base of the neck, the classic surface landmark for counting vertebrae. Its transverse foramina are small and usually transmit only accessory veins (not the vertebral artery), and it lacks the uncinate processes of the typical cervical vertebrae — an easy identification point.

R Recall — cervical vertebrae
  • Cervical signature — the transverse foramen (carries the vertebral artery)
  • Typical cervical — small wide body, triangular foramen, bifid spine, uncinate processes
  • Atlas (C1) — no body, no spinous process → the "yes" joint
  • Axis (C2) — bears the dens → the "no" rotation pivot
  • C7 — vertebra prominens, long non-bifid spinous process (landmark)
§2Thoracic region

Thoracic vertebrae (T1–T12)

The rib-bearing region — built to rotate, not to flex.

Twelve vertebrae defined by one job: articulating with the ribs. Their costal facets and near-vertical, coronally-oriented facets make rotation the dominant movement while limiting flexion/extension — the opposite emphasis to the neck.

Exam hook · the thoracic identification checklist

Identify a thoracic vertebra by its rib connections: a heart-shaped body carrying costal facets (or demifacets) for the head of a rib; a costal facet on the transverse process for the rib tubercle; a small circular vertebral foramen; and a long, slender, downward-sloping spinous process that overlaps the vertebra below (so the tip of one spine lies at the body of the next — important when counting or doing a thoracic tap).

Why · the ribs and facets gate the movement

The thoracic facets sit in a near-coronal, vertical plane, and the attached rib cage plus overlapping spinous processes splint the region. Together these limit flexion, extension and lateral flexion but permit a good deal of rotation. This is the mirror image of the lumbar region (§3), where sagittal facets allow flexion/extension but block rotation — a favourite compare-and-contrast question.

Why · the ends blend into their neighbours

The transitional thoracic vertebrae borrow features from adjacent regions: T1–T4 show some cervical traits (T1 has a long, almost horizontal spine, a complete superior costal facet and a demifacet); T9–T12 show some lumbar traits and the costal facets simplify (T9 one demifacet; T10–T12 a single full facet each as the lower ribs articulate with a single vertebra). The facet pattern is how you pin an atypical thoracic level.

R Recall — thoracic vertebrae
  • Thoracic signature — costal facets (body + transverse process) for the ribs
  • Body shape — heart-shaped; foramen small and circular
  • Spinous process — long, sloping down, overlaps the vertebra below
  • Movement allowed — mainly rotation (coronal facets + rib cage limit flexion)
§3Lumbar region

Lumbar vertebrae (L1–L5)

The load-bearers — massive bodies, sagittal facets, no rotation.

Five big vertebrae carrying the most weight. Their sagittally-oriented facets are the key: they allow generous flexion and extension but lock rotation, which protects the lumbar discs — the ones that herniate most.

Exam hook · the lumbar identification checklist

Identify a lumbar vertebra by size and facet plane: a massive kidney-shaped body (built for weight-bearing), a triangular vertebral foramen, long slender transverse processes, and crucially articular processes oriented in the sagittal plane. No costal facets and no transverse foramen — their absence is itself the clue.

Why · sagittal facets = flexion yes, rotation no

The sagittal facet orientation is the examinable mechanical point: facets lying in the sagittal plane interlock against twisting, so the lumbar spine flexes and extends freely but barely rotates. That protects the discs from shear — but it also means the pars interarticularis (the bony bridge between superior and inferior facets) takes repetitive stress, and its stress fracture (spondylolysis, which can progress to spondylolisthesis) is a classic lumbar lesion, as covered in L17.

R Recall — lumbar vertebrae
  • Lumbar signature — massive kidney-shaped body; sagittal facets
  • Facets allow — flexion/extension but block rotation
  • Absent features — no costal facets, no transverse foramen
  • Stress point — the pars interarticularis → spondylolysis
§4Sacrum, coccyx & comparison

Sacrum, coccyx & regional comparison

The fused base — and a side-by-side of all five regions.

The column ends in two fused blocks that trade all mobility for a rigid weight-transfer platform, then the lecture lines up the regions so you can read each region's job straight off its shape.

Why · fusion buys a weight-transfer platform

The sacrum is five fused vertebrae forming a wedge that transmits body weight from the spine to the pelvis across the sacroiliac joints, and its anterior and posterior sacral foramina transmit the sacral spinal nerve rami. The coccyx is three to four vestigial fused vertebrae — small, but a real attachment site for pelvic-floor muscles and ligaments. Fusion is the whole point: the base of the column sacrifices movement for rigid, reliable load transfer.

Exam hook · read the region off the shape, and the landmarks

Put the regions side by side and the logic is: cervical = small + transverse foramen + bifid spine (mobility); thoracic = costal facets + heart-shaped body (ribs, rotation); lumbar = massive body + sagittal facets (load, flexion). For surface anatomy, the counting landmarks are C7 vertebra prominens, the spine of T3 ≈ the scapular spine, T7 ≈ the inferior scapular angle, and L4 ≈ the iliac crest (supracristal plane) — the level used to find the space for a lumbar puncture (L20).

R Recall — sacrum, coccyx & comparison
  • Sacrum — 5 fused vertebrae; transfers weight via the sacroiliac joints
  • Coccyx — 3–4 vestigial fused vertebrae; pelvic-floor attachment
  • Read the region — cervical=transverse foramen, thoracic=costal facets, lumbar=sagittal facets
  • Landmark — L4 ≈ the iliac crest (supracristal plane)
